summary: Morocco grants visa-free entry to a long list of nationalities — including the US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia, Japan, Brazil, Mexico, Russia and China — and runs an official eVisa system (acces-maroc.ma) for several other nationalities; the dirham is a closed currency, so bring foreign cash or cards and change money inside the country.

conditionalWaivers.text: Visa-required nationals holding a valid multiple-entry sticker visa (90+ days remaining) from the US, Schengen, the UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia, Japan, Norway or New Zealand qualify for Morocco's eVisa (electronic authorisations like ESTA do not count). So do visa-required nationals living in the EU, the US, Australia, Canada, the UK, Japan, Norway, New Zealand, the UAE or Switzerland with a residence card or permit valid at least 180 days on the date of application.

source.name: Accès Maroc — eVisa terms of use (general information note)

fee.notes: Standard track, decided in 3–7 working days. The Express track costs 1,100 MAD and is decided in 1–3 working days. Both amounts are the portal's own price list, charged before the application is processed.

source.name: Accès Maroc — eVisa price list (the portal's published tariff: Standard and Express)

fee.notes: No fee: the portal exempts this nationality from the eVisa charge, on both the Standard and the Express track.

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 3 months from the date you arrive in Morocco. Make sure it is not damaged: travellers with damaged passports have been refused entry.

source.name: UK FCDO — Morocco travel advice, entry requirements

vaccinations.name: Polio
vaccinations.text: If you arrive from a polio-affected country, you must carry a certificate proving you have had a polio vaccination.

source.name: UK FCDO — Morocco travel advice, entry requirements

travelInsurance.text: eVisa holders must be able to show hospital and medical repatriation insurance covering their whole stay when they arrive. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it.

source.name: Kingdom of Morocco eVisa portal (acces-maroc.ma) — Conditions of use of the eVisa

onwardTicket.text: eVisa holders must be able to show a return ticket at the border on arrival. No official source states a ticket requirement for visa-exempt visitors.

source.name: Kingdom of Morocco eVisa portal (acces-maroc.ma) — Conditions of use of the eVisa

proofOfFunds.text: eVisa holders must be able to show means of support on arrival: an international bank card, or more than EUR 70 in cash per person per day of the stay.

source.name: Kingdom of Morocco eVisa portal (acces-maroc.ma) — Conditions of use of the eVisa

currencyLimits.text: The Moroccan dirham (MAD) is a closed currency: you may bring in or take out at most 2,000 MAD. Foreign currency can be imported freely but amounts of 100,000 MAD equivalent or more must be declared; keep exchange receipts to convert leftover dirhams back before departure.

source.name: Moroccan Customs Administration (ADII) — foreigners visiting Morocco: currency and exchange

notes: Moroccan Customs says importing drones and other remote-controlled unmanned aircraft is prohibited without an import licence from the department responsible for foreign trade; without one, the drone is held in customs storage for up to 45 days pending regularisation and is then treated as abandoned.

Moroccan Customs' duty-free allowance for each adult visitor: 200 g of manufactured tobacco, one 1-litre bottle of wine, one 1-litre bottle of spirits, one 150 ml bottle of perfume and one 250 ml bottle of eau de toilette.
Cultural goods — works of art, collectors' items and antiques — may only leave Morocco with a certificate from the Moroccan department responsible for cultural affairs, according to Moroccan Customs.

payments.text: The Government of Canada says credit cards and traveller's cheques are accepted in certain stores and restaurants in urban centres and in major hotels. The dirham cannot be exchanged outside Morocco, and it is illegal to take dirhams out of the country, so exchange only as much as you need; unused dirhams can be converted at the airport exchange counter on departure with proof of your original purchase.

safety.text: Petty crime is common in tourist areas, especially in the medinas and on beaches: pickpocketing, bag-snatching and drive-by motorcycle theft. People posing as official guides often harass tourists, so use only guides with an official badge. There is occasional violent crime, including knife attacks on tourists in major cities and along beaches, so avoid quiet areas after dark. Terrorists are likely to try to carry out attacks in Morocco, including in places visited by foreigners.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Morocco travel advice (safety and security)

bestTimeToVisit.text: No official seasonal guidance. The Government of Canada says Morocco's rainy season usually runs from November to March, when flash floods can occur frequently and are especially dangerous in the High Atlas valleys.

idp.text: Morocco is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Morocco is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Morocco yet.

tips.text: The dirham is a closed currency. Moroccan Customs allows at most 2,000 MAD to be carried in or out of Morocco, so change money inside the country and convert leftovers back (keep exchange receipts) before you leave.

The UK Foreign Office says people posing as official tourist guides commonly harass tourists; if you use a guide in a medina, make sure they have an official badge and permission from the local authority. The Government of Canada advises hiring only official guides recommended by hotels, travel agencies or local tourist authorities.

Moroccan Customs prohibits bringing in a drone without an import licence from the department responsible for foreign trade; unlicensed drones are held for up to 45 days and then treated as abandoned. To fly one, the UK Foreign Office says you also need permission from the Directorate General for Civil Aviation.

During Ramadan the Government of Canada advises refraining from drinking, eating and smoking in public between sunrise and sunset; the UK Foreign Office notes that doing so in the daytime may cause offence.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Morocco?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Morocco without a visa: Morocco's Foreign Ministry lists the United States as exempt, but does not state how long the stay may last, and no official source we could read does. Your passport is stamped on entry, so check the stamp.

faq.question: How long can EU and UK citizens stay in Morocco?
faq.answer: UK citizens can stay visa-free for up to 90 days for tourism, according to the UK government; to stay longer they must request an extension at a Moroccan police station. EU citizens are also visa-exempt, but Morocco's Foreign Ministry list gives a stay length only for Hungary (90 days), and no other official source we could read states one.

faq.question: Can I buy Moroccan dirhams before my trip?
faq.answer: Effectively no. The UK Foreign Office says the dirham is a closed, non-convertible currency that cannot easily be exchanged outside Morocco, and Moroccan Customs allows at most 2,000 MAD to be carried in or out. Change money at banks or official exchange bureaux in Morocco and keep receipts: the Government of Canada says unused dirhams can be converted at the airport exchange counter on departure with proof of your original purchase.

faq.question: Who needs Morocco's eVisa and where do you apply?
faq.answer: Most Western and East Asian passports, and several Latin American ones (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru), do not need any visa. The eVisa is open to citizens of India, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Brunei, Jordan, Israel, Benin and Guatemala, and to other visa-required travelers who hold a valid multiple-entry visa from the US, Schengen, the UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia, Japan, Norway or New Zealand. Check eligibility and apply at the official portal acces-maroc.ma; the standard track is decided in 3–7 working days and the express track in 1–3. Travelers not eligible online apply at a Moroccan embassy.
